steps: MRI + MR venography (exclude mass/venous sinus thrombosis), then LP to confirm raised opening pressure with normal CSF.
Weight loss is central; consider a GLP-1 receptor agonist if unable to lose weight by diet.
Acetazolamide first-line (250-500 mg bid) to lower CSF production; topiramate is the next agent if ineffective.
Formal perimetry and urgent ophthalmology if visual loss; severe/progressive loss needs CSF diversion (lumboperitoneal shunt) or optic-nerve-sheath fenestration.

drugRefs.dose: 250–500 mg twice daily, up-titrated as tolerated (up to ~1–2 g/day)
drugRefs.why: First-line agent — reduces CSF production and intracranial pressure; the mainstay medical therapy alongside weight loss.
Alternative when acetazolamide is ineffective/not tolerated; has weak carbonic-anhydrase-inhibiting activity and promotes appetite suppression/weight loss.

refs: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22e — Idiopathic Intracranial Hypertension
Consensus Guidelines on Idiopathic Intracranial Hypertension (Mollan et al., JNNP 2018)
Idiopathic Intracranial Hypertension Treatment Trial (IIHTT), JAMA 2014

decision.label: Acetazolamide + weight loss; urgent ophthalmology if visual loss

confirm: Headache + visual disturbance with papilloedema, typically a young obese woman; normal imaging; LP opening pressure raised with normal CSF.
